statement: In the statistical models of the two studies read that measured both agents (a driving simulator, and records of drivers in fatal crashes), lane weave or the odds of a recorded unsafe driver action were higher with cannabis and alcohol together than with either alone, by about the sum of the two separate effects and not clearly more than the sum. In the simulator (18 healthy adults who smoke cannabis occasionally, driving after every condition in random order), lane weave rose with blood THC by 0.26 cm per µg/L (standard error 0.07) and with breath alcohol by 0.42 cm per 0.01 g/210 L (0.15), both modelled for the time of the drive, and no interaction term was selected; from a drug-free median of 31.4 cm, the model gives +1.3 cm for THC 5 µg/L, +2.1 cm for breath alcohol 0.05 g/210 L and +3.4 cm for both, while lane departures and lateral acceleration rose with alcohol but not with THC. Among 150,010 drivers of cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks in fatal US crashes (1991–2008) with blood tests for alcohol and drugs, a police-recorded unsafe driver action was linked to both: for a 45-year-old man with no other drugs or driving record, about 64 in 100 had one at a blood alcohol of 0.05 g/100 mL without THC and 66 in 100 with it, and 70 and 71 in 100 at 0.08 (editors' calculation); the odds ratio for THC fell as alcohol rose, from 1.165 (95% CI 1.082–1.255) at 0.00 to about 1.09 at 0.05 and 1.05 at 0.08 (editors' calculation). Both studies differ from driving on a road. The simulator measured lane weave in healthy volunteers, its combined values are sums by construction, 18 people were analysed, and achieved THC overlapped between its two cannabis doses. The crash analysis compares drivers who were already in fatal crashes, with and without a recorded unsafe action, so it measures neither crash risk nor impairment; it rests on a yes/no blood result for THC in about one in five eligible drivers, and prints no test of what THC adds to alcohol at 0.05 or 0.08. A meta-analysis reports a higher odds ratio for the combination than for cannabis alone in every study that assessed it, without numbers, which does not separate additive from more-than-additive effects. Both papers describe other simulator and on-road studies as disagreeing on whether the combination exceeds the sum; these were not read. Neither paper reports how impaired the drivers felt, neither gives the risk to one driver, and cause is not shown.
plain: Does cannabis with alcohol make driving worse than either alone? In a driving simulator, 18 healthy adults weaved a little more in their lane with cannabis and a little more with alcohol. With both, the extra weave was about the two added together: 3.4 cm more with both (THC 5 µg/L in blood, breath alcohol 0.05), against 2.1 cm more with alcohol alone, on a usual weave of about 31 cm. In US records of drivers in fatal crashes who had a blood test, about 64 in 100 at a blood alcohol of 0.05 had a recorded unsafe driving action, and about 66 in 100 if cannabis was also found. At 0.08 it was about 70 and 71 in 100, so cannabis added less as alcohol rose. Neither study measured crash risk on real roads, and a positive cannabis test shows it was in the blood, not that a driver was impaired. Other studies disagree on whether the two together do more than the sum of each.
population: Adults who drive: 18 healthy adults aged 21–37 who smoke cannabis occasionally (driving-simulator study; 19 drove, one excluded after the fact), and 150,010 drivers aged 20 or older of cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks in fatal US crashes, 1991–2008, who had blood tests for alcohol and drugs (149,006 in the main analysis)
exposure: Cannabis together with alcohol: vaporized cannabis with blood THC modelled for the time of the drive, and alcohol drunk before it (study conditions, simulator); a THC-positive blood test with blood alcohol 0.00–0.08 g/100 mL (crash records)
comparator: Alcohol alone, cannabis alone, or neither (placebo drive in the simulator; blood alcohol 0.00 with no THC detected in the crash records)
outcome: Lane weave in a driving simulator (standard deviation of lateral position, cm); a police-recorded potentially unsafe driver action among drivers in fatal crashes
magnitude: Driving simulator (Hartman et al., 2015; 18 healthy adults analysed of 19 who drove; lane weave as standard deviation of lateral position, SDLP; model predictions at 55 mph on a straight road; drug-free median 31.4 cm, between-person range 24.7–44.8): blood THC 5 µg/L +1.3 cm (4.1%); breath alcohol 0.05 g/210 L +2.1 cm (6.7%); both +3.4 cm (11%), the same as breath alcohol 0.08 alone (+3.4 cm); combined values are sums because the selected model has no interaction term. Alcohol, not THC, raised lane departures per minute (+35% at 0.05 g/210 L, +55% at 0.08) and maximum lateral acceleration in events without sharp turns (+9.5% and +15%); neither drug changed steering-angle variability. By administered condition (18 drivers each; study conditions; no tests or intervals given), mean SDLP was placebo 28.8 cm, alcohol alone 32.3 (+12%), low THC alone 31.3, high THC alone 31.2, low THC with alcohol 34.2 (+19%) and high THC with alcohol 32.2 (+12%); in a mixed model by achieved THC group the THC-by-alcohol term had P = 0.24 (low power, the authors say). Fatal-crash drivers (Dubois et al., 2015; 150,010 drivers with blood tests for alcohol and drugs, 149,006 in the main analysis; a recorded unsafe driver action as a proxy for responsibility; model for a male driver aged 45 with no other drugs or driving record; share with an unsafe action calculated by the editors from the printed predicted odds): 52 in 100 at blood alcohol 0.00 without THC and 56 in 100 with THC; 64 and 66 in 100 at 0.05; 70 and 71 in 100 at 0.08. Odds ratios against no alcohol and no THC: THC alone 1.16 (1.08–1.26); alcohol 0.05 alone 1.66 (1.63–1.69) and with THC 1.81 (1.70–1.93); alcohol 0.08 alone 2.17 (2.11–2.23) and with THC 2.28 (2.13–2.44). The THC-by-blood-alcohol term was 0.987 (0.981–0.994) per 0.01, so the odds ratio for THC falls as alcohol rises: about 1.17 at 0.00, 1.09 at 0.05 and 1.05 at 0.08 (editors' calculation, no interval). The combined odds ratio is close to the sum of the two separate excesses (about 1.83 at 0.05 and 2.34 at 0.08, editors' calculation) and below their product (1.93 and 2.53). Asbridge et al. (2012): in every study that assessed cannabis with alcohol, the odds ratio for the combination was higher than for cannabis alone; no numbers are given.

These are 0.8% and 1.3% of the drug-free median SDLP (31.4 cm) per unit.

evidence.extracted: Nineteen healthy adults drove (13 men, 6 women; ages 21–37; occasional cannabis smokers); participant 12 was excluded from all driving analyses after the fact, leaving 18. Six conditions (placebo, two strengths of vaporized cannabis, each with placebo or alcohol) in randomized order at least a week apart; a 45-minute night drive in a driving simulator began 0.5–1.3 hours after cannabis dosing. The authors note that participants know their driving is observed, that frequent smokers show tolerance to some effects, and that the model-selection procedure was used to describe the data; they do not regard use of a simulator rather than a road as a significant limitation. The paper reports no rating of how impaired participants felt.

evidence.extracted: The paper describes earlier work as inconsistent on whether cannabis and alcohol together act additively or synergistically: a simulator study found a lane-position increase only with the combination (Ronen 2010), another found separate effects and no interaction (Lenné 2010), and an on-road study found larger lane-position increases with low amounts of both combined than with either alone (Robbe 1998; Ramaekers 2000). Second-hand: these studies were not read for this library.

The Discussion puts alcohol at .05 and .08 at 66% and 117% greater odds and with THC 81% and 128%. Table 3 checked on the rendered page. Editors' calculation: odds divided by one plus odds gives about 52 and 56 in 100 at BAC 0.00, 64 and 66 at .05 and 70 and 71 at .08 (without and with THC); the ratio of predicted odds with to without THC is 1.17, 1.09 and 1.05; the combined odds ratio is about the sum of the excesses (1.83 and 2.34) and below the product (1.93 and 2.53). The constant (0.140) and sex coefficient (−0.074) reproduce the printed 1.07 only if other covariates are at reference values.

Outcome: a police-recorded potentially unsafe driver action (proxy for responsibility), so the comparison is among drivers already in fatal crashes. THC is a yes/no blood marker of unstated analyte with no concentration, dose or timing; the authors note THC can remain in the blood for hours or days and that FARS does not say why THC was present. The paper reports no rating of how impaired drivers felt. Appendix 1 (comparison of tested and untested drivers) is not in the manuscript.

evidence.extracted: The paper describes the effect of alcohol and cannabis together as appearing greater than that of either alone, generally additive (seven sources cited) or possibly synergistic (six), with some research finding no additive effect (three); at low alcohol with small cannabis amounts it calls the results inconsistent: one on-road study found no significant difference in a driving proficiency test against drug-free driving, although visual search at intersections fell by 3% (p = .041), while another found severe impairment with the combination and only minor to moderate impairment with each alone. Second-hand: these studies were not read for this library.

evidence.locator: Results › Primary and secondary analyses, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: In all studies that assessed cannabis in conjunction with alcohol, the estimated odds ratio for the combination was higher than for cannabis alone; the authors take this to suggest synergy, cite four sources and give no estimates. The comparison is with cannabis alone, so it does not separate an additive from a more-than-additive combination, since alcohol raises the odds on its own. The review's pooled estimates are for cannabis-only drivers (blood THC with no alcohol or other drug).

risk_of_bias.note: The crash analysis is ROBINS-E high on its card (selection into blood testing: about one in five eligible drivers; a police-coded proxy for responsibility; a data-driven step-down model) and the simulator study RoB 2 some concerns (a participant excluded after the fact, stepwise model selection, no intervals on the stated equivalences); one downgrade for both together.

inconsistency.note: The two studies read agree on the pattern. Other simulator and on-road studies, known only from how the two papers describe them, disagree on whether the combination exceeds the sum; they were not read, so they are not scored here (scoring would not change the rating, which is at its floor), and they are why the status is mixed.

indirectness.note: Neither source measures impairment on a road or the chance of a crash: the simulator measures lane weave in healthy occasional smokers, the crash records measure a recorded unsafe action among drivers already in fatal crashes, and THC is a yes/no blood marker there.

imprecision.note: Not scored because the claim says not clearly more than the sum, not no interaction: 18 people were analysed, and no interval or test is printed for what THC adds to alcohol at 0.05 or 0.08; the crash intervals for single odds ratios are narrow.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the odds ratios are below 3 and confounding runs towards both sides.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the gradients with blood alcohol and THC in the data are model outputs in both studies, and the claim is about the combination.

plausible_confounding.note: Not applied: who chooses to drive after cannabis, and with alcohol, could push either way.

grade.reasoning: Two sources of different kinds, both read in full. The real-world half rests on a records-based case-control analysis (starts low); the other on a within-person simulator study with randomized condition order, which would start high. The claim is rated from the weaker link, so it starts low. Risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 (see the domain notes); inconsistency, imprecision and publication bias 0; large effect, dose-response and plausible confounding not applied. If the simulator study alone were taken as the link, it would start high and lose 1 for risk of bias, 2 for indirectness (lane weave in healthy occasional smokers is two steps from impairment or crashes on a road) and 1 for imprecision (18 people, no interval on the equivalences), which is also very low. Relation: is associated with; the crash analysis cannot separate cannabis from who chooses to drive after it, and neither source shows cause. The claim does not say the combination is additive in general: the simulator's combined values are sums by construction, and the crash model's product term tests departure from multiplication, so near-additivity in the crash data is the editors' arithmetic on Table 3, which holds up to about BAC 0.04 with the combination a little below the sum from 0.05. Status: mixed. The two studies read agree, but both papers describe the wider literature on the combination as inconsistent (additive, more than additive, or no more than alcohol), and the library's rule for mixed is several studies with inconsistent findings and no adequate explanation; the older on-road studies would be the first to read, and could move the status to contested. The Rogeberg and Elvik re-analysis, read for this library, studies cannabis alone with alcohol controlled or adjusted and does not address the combination.

verification.flag_note: Not read: Rogeberg 2019 (culpability-design meta-analysis, 10.1016/j.aap.2018.11.011, open access); Dubois Appendix 1 and Rogeberg Appendix S1 (not in the PDFs); the older simulator and on-road studies of the combination (Robbe 1998, Ramaekers 2000, Lamers 2001, Lenné 2010, Ronen 2010), known only from how Hartman and Dubois describe them; Li et al. 2012, Elvik 2013 and Bédard 2007; the Hartman supplements and registry record (NCT01620177); the Thai companion papers on subjective and cognitive effects; Liechti 2006 and Miró 2017 on GHB with alcohol. No study read asks whether drivers or patients felt impaired (Ronen 2010 on perceived effects and Verster and Roth 2012 on drivers' own predictions are named in the Hartman reference list). Status mixed rests on how the two papers describe the wider literature; reading the older on-road studies could move it to contested (a debate box would then be needed).
